passages.t: The favored son and the robe
passages.happening:
Jacob lives in Canaan, where his father had lived. “This is the account of Jacob” (verse 2).

Joseph is seventeen. He tends the flock with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, “and he brought their father a bad report about them” (verse 2).

“Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors” (verse 3).

“When Joseph's brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
This heading opens the last great part of Genesis. It is called ‘the account of Jacob’, but its main character is Joseph, with Judah close behind. It runs to the end of the book.

Joseph is Rachel's first son, the son of the wife Jacob loved. Rachel has died. Now Jacob pours that love into her boy, and he does it openly.

The robe is famous. The Hebrew words are uncertain. ‘A robe of many colors’ follows the old Greek translation and the King James Version. Others take the words to mean a robe with long sleeves, reaching to the wrists and ankles. Either way it was not work clothing. You cannot herd sheep in it. The only other place the phrase appears is for the robe worn by a king's daughters (2 Samuel 13:18). The robe says: this son is set apart.

And Joseph carries tales. He brings his father a bad report about his brothers. We are not told whether it was true. But the favored son is also the one who tells on the others.

The brothers hate him. They cannot even say ‘hello’ to him kindly. The Hebrew says they could not speak to him ‘for peace’, the word shalom.

Favoritism has run through this family for three generations. Isaac loved Esau, and Rebekah loved Jacob (25:28). Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah (29:30). Now Jacob loves one son more than the rest. Every time, it poisons the family.
passages.later: The Bible warns against favoritism. James writes, “My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism” (James 2:1). Paul tells fathers, “Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21).
passages.hard:
A word for anyone who grew up as the child a parent did not favor, or who watched a brother or sister receive the love they longed for. The pain of Joseph's brothers is real, even though what they did with it was evil. If you know that hurt, it was not your fault. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If the hurt is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.

And a word for parents. Every parent feels closer to one child on some days. Jacob's sin was to show it, to dress it, and to build a home around it. Children see the rankings in a family, even when no one says them aloud.
passages.asks: Jacob loved one son more and made it plain. Ask whether anyone in your home, your church or your work can see that you favor some over others. Then ask what that is doing to the ones you pass over, and to the one you favor.

passages.happening:
Joseph has a dream and tells his brothers. “We were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine” (verse 7).

“Do you intend to reign over us?” they ask. “So they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements” (verse 8).

He has another dream: “the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me” (verse 9). His father rebukes him: “Will your mother and brothers and I actually come and bow down to the ground before you?” (verse 10).

“And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept in mind what he had said” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world dreams were taken seriously. People believed a god might speak through them. Egyptians even wrote books on how to read dreams. A dream that came twice in two pictures was thought to be especially sure. Joseph himself will say so later (41:32).

The sheaves are bundles of cut grain. In the first dream the brothers' bundles bow to Joseph's. In the second the whole family bows: the sun and moon are his father and mother, and the eleven stars his brothers. Rachel has already died (35:19), which shows these are pictures, not a literal forecast.

The dreams may well come from God. They will come true in Egypt. But Joseph is seventeen, and he tells them to the very people they will hurt. He tells his brothers, who already hate him, that they will bow to him. Then he does it again.

Notice the father. Jacob scolds him in public, but in private he ‘kept in mind’ what Joseph said. He wonders what it means.

And notice the word ‘jealous’. Hate grows step by step in this chapter: they hated him (verse 4), they hated him more (verse 5), they hated him even more (verse 8), they were jealous (verse 11). Soon they will want him dead.
passages.later:
The dream comes true years later in Egypt, when Joseph's brothers come to buy grain: “they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground” (Genesis 42:6).

Mary, the mother of Jesus, is described in almost the same way as Jacob: “Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart” (Luke 2:19).
passages.asks: Joseph had a true dream and told it in the worst way. Ask whether you have ever been right about something and still hurt people by how you said it. Then ask whether jealousy is growing in you step by step toward someone.

passages.happening:
The brothers take the flocks to pasture near Shechem. Jacob sends Joseph to see how they are (verses 12-14). A man finds Joseph wandering in the fields and tells him they have gone on to Dothan (verses 15-17).

The brothers see him in the distance, “and before he arrived, they plotted to kill him” (verse 18). “Here comes that dreamer!” they say (verse 19). “Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits” (verse 20).

Reuben stops them: “Let us not take his life” (verse 21). “Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him” (verse 22). He means to rescue Joseph later.

When Joseph arrives, “they stripped him of his robe” (verse 23). They throw him into the pit. “Now the pit was empty, with no water in it” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Shechem is a long way north of Hebron, where Jacob lives. It is also the place where the brothers killed every man in a city (chapter 34). Jacob sends his favored son alone to the brothers who hate him. He does not seem to see the danger.

Dothan lay further north, near a pass on the trade road that ran from Gilead, east of the Jordan, down toward Egypt. That detail will matter.

The brothers see the robe from far off. They call him ‘that dreamer’, which in Hebrew is mocking, like saying ‘the master of dreams’. Their plan reveals what they hate most: ‘Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams.’

Reuben is the eldest. He has already shamed his father (35:22). Perhaps he hopes to win back his place by saving Joseph. He means well, but he does not stand up openly. He offers a half-measure and goes away.

The pit is a cistern, a bottle-shaped hole cut into rock to store rainwater. It is narrow at the top and wide below. No one can climb out. This one is dry. It is not a well where a boy might drown. It is a prison.

The first thing they do is strip off the robe. The sign of their father's love is the thing they hate most.
passages.later:
Years later the brothers remember this day: “We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen” (Genesis 42:21). Genesis does not tell us Joseph's cries here. We learn them only through his brothers' guilty memory.

The prophet Jeremiah was also let down into a cistern with no water in it, only mud (Jeremiah 38:6). And Jesus told a parable of tenants who saw the owner's son coming and said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance” (Matthew 21:38).
passages.asks: Reuben wanted to save Joseph but would not stand against his brothers openly. Ask where you know something is wrong and are hoping to fix it quietly later. Then ask what it would cost to speak now.

passages.happening:
“And as they sat down to eat a meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead” (verse 25). Their camels carry spices, balm and myrrh down to Egypt.

Judah speaks. “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?” (verse 26). “Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh” (verse 27). The others agree.

“So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Read verse 25 slowly. They throw their brother into a pit, and then they sit down to eat. The coldness is the point.

Gilead is the hill country east of the Jordan. Balm and myrrh are sweet-smelling resins from trees. Egypt prized them for medicine, perfume and the care of the dead.

Judah's words sound almost kind: ‘he is our brother, our own flesh.’ But listen to his first question: ‘What profit?’ He saves Joseph's life by turning him into money. Judah will change in the chapters ahead. Here he is the one who sells his brother.

A shekel was a weight of silver, not a coin. Twenty shekels was a real price for a young man. Israel's later law set the value of a male aged five to twenty at exactly twenty shekels (Leviticus 27:5). The Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen argued, in an article of 1995, that twenty shekels also matches the usual price of a slave in the time of Hammurabi, around the 1700s BC, and that prices were higher in later centuries. Others doubt that prices can date the story. The book page on Genesis sets out the debate over dates.

Who sold Joseph? The chapter names both Ishmaelites and Midianites. Readers explain this in three main ways. Some take them as the same traders: Judges 8:24 calls Midianites ‘Ishmaelites’, perhaps a general name for desert traders. Others read verse 28 to say that Midianites passed by and pulled Joseph out themselves while the brothers ate, then sold him; that would explain why Reuben finds the pit empty. Many scholars think two tellings of the story have been woven together. On every reading, the Bible holds the brothers responsible. Joseph will say to them, ‘I am Joseph, your brother, the one you sold into Egypt’ (45:4), and they do not deny it.
passages.later:
Israel's law treated selling a person as a crime worthy of death: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16). Paul lists “slave traders” among those whom God's law condemns (1 Timothy 1:10).

A psalm remembers that God sent a man ahead of his people: “Joseph, sold as a slave” (Psalm 105:17). Amos condemns those who “sell the righteous for silver” (Amos 2:6). Jesus was betrayed for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15).
passages.hard:
Human trafficking is the buying, selling or holding of people for forced work or for sex. It is evil, and it still happens today. Joseph's brothers did it to their own brother, and the Bible names it a crime.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Judah asked, ‘What profit?’ and turned his brother into silver. Ask where you are tempted to treat a person as something to use or to profit from. Then ask who might be paying for the things you buy, and whether you want to know.

passages.t: A robe dipped in goat's blood
passages.happening:
Reuben comes back and finds the pit empty. He tears his clothes. “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?” (verses 29-30).

“Then they took Joseph's robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood” (verse 31). They send it to their father: “We found this. Examine it to see whether it is your son's robe or not” (verse 32).

Jacob says, “It is my son's robe! A vicious animal has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!” (verse 33). He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and mourns many days (verse 34). His children try to comfort him, “but he refused to be comforted” (verse 35). “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son” (verse 35).

“Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
The first hearers would catch the echo at once. Long ago Jacob deceived his own father with a young goat. He served Isaac goat meat dressed up as game, and wore goat skins on his arms to pass as Esau (27:9, 16). Now his sons deceive him with a young goat's blood. The trick he played comes back to him.

Notice the cruel words, ‘Examine it.’ They do not say Joseph is dead. They let their father say it. He ‘recognizes’ the robe, and he draws the false conclusion they wanted. That word ‘recognize’ will return in the next chapter, and again in Egypt.

Tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth, rough cloth made of goat's hair, were signs of deep mourning. Sheol is the place of the dead. This is the first time the Bible names it. Jacob means he will grieve until he dies.

And the brothers ‘try to comfort’ him, knowing the truth. They watch their father's grief for years and say nothing.

The last verse turns to Egypt. Joseph is sold again. Potiphar is an officer of Pharaoh, Egypt's king. The boy in the robe is now a slave in a foreign land. God is not named once in this chapter. But the story is moving.
passages.later:
Years later Joseph tells his brothers what God was doing: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). This does not excuse the brothers. It says their evil was not the last word.

Stephen tells the story in Acts: “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him” (Acts 7:9).
passages.asks: Jacob was paid back in his own coin, and his sons hid the truth for years. Ask whether there is a lie you are living with, that someone else is paying for. Then ask what it would mean to tell the truth before it comes out on its own.
